title: Liberalisation and Economic Reforms

cards.h: 1991: the turn from plan to market
cards.b:
In mid-1991 India nearly defaulted on its foreign debt. Foreign exchange reserves had fallen to cover only a few weeks of imports. The government pledged gold abroad to raise funds. In this crisis, the new government of P.V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, launched reforms.

The reforms replaced the licence raj with a market-friendly economy. Growth rose, poverty fell, but inequality grew.

Political science asks distinct questions: how did a democracy carry out reform without a mandate? Who gained and who lost? How did reforms change the State, parties and federalism? The UPSC regularly asks about the "politics of economic reforms".

• New Industrial Policy (24 July 1991): licensing ended for most industries; MRTP restrictions eased; public sector reserved list cut.
  • Budget of 24 July 1991: devaluation (earlier that month), tariff cuts, and the start of tax reform.
  • Foreign investment: automatic approval in many sectors.
  • Financial sector: the Narasimham Committee (1991) led banking reforms; SEBI got statutory powers (1992).
  • India joined the WTO in 1995.

Rob Jenkins, Democratic Politics and Economic Reform in India (1999)

Reform by stealth: leaders presented changes as continuity, used federalism to push hard choices to states, and paid off losers. Democratic institutions helped, not hindered, reform.

Ashutosh Varshney, "Mass Politics or Elite Politics?" (1999)

Reforms that touch elites (trade, industry) passed easily; reforms touching mass politics (labour laws, farm subsidies, power tariffs) were hard, since voters care about them.

Atul Kohli, Poverty Amid Plenty in the New India (2012)

The State moved to a pro-business alliance with big capital from the 1980s, before 1991. Growth came, but with weak job creation and inequality.

Bhagwati and Panagariya vs Drèze and Sen (2013)

Why Growth Matters stresses growth to fund welfare; An Uncertain Glory stresses public investment in health and education.

• Growth: average growth rose to about 6-7% a year from the 1990s to the 2010s.
  • Poverty: fell sharply. By the Tendulkar method, poverty fell from about 37% (2004-05) to about 22% (2011-12).
  • Services and IT boomed; a middle class grew.
  • Inequality rose; manufacturing jobs lagged ("jobless growth").
  • Agriculture grew slowly; rural distress persisted.
  • Regional gaps: western and southern states gained more than many northern and eastern ones.

Political effects: states became competitors for investment; Chief Ministers' role in economic policy grew; coalitions limited big-bang reform; the welfare state expanded through rights-based laws (RTI, MGNREGA, RTE, NFSA) in 2005-13.

• Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016).
  • Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes on 8 November 2016.
  • GST from 1 July 2017 (101st Amendment), with GST Council. In September 2025, the Council simplified it to two main rates (5% and 18%) from 22 September 2025.
  • Direct benefit transfer through the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, mobile).
  • Production-linked incentives (2020) and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
  • Corporate tax cut (2019).
  • Farm laws (2020), repealed in 2021 after protests.
  • Four labour codes, in force from 21 November 2025.

Pattern: reforms with concentrated losers (farmers, unions) remained the hardest, confirming Varshney's mass-elite distinction.

Supporters: reforms raised growth, cut poverty, modernised industry, and integrated India with the world. Bhagwati and Panagariya argue growth is the main poverty-fighting tool.

Critics:

  • Left: crony capitalism, privatisation of public assets, weakening of labour rights.
  • Kohli: pro-business, not pro-market; the State favours big firms.
  • Drèze and Sen: neglect of health and education keeps India behind East Asia.
  • Environmental critics: fast growth damaged forests and rivers.
  • Federal concern: GST reduced states' fiscal autonomy.

A balanced answer: reforms were necessary and successful in growth, but the social and institutional side (education, health, jobs, regulation) needed equal attention.

• Party convergence: all major parties accepted reforms in office, even if they opposed them in opposition. Yogendra Yadav and Suhas Palshikar noted a convergence on economic policy.
  • Welfare politics: parties now compete through targeted schemes and cash transfers.
  • Regulatory state: new regulators (SEBI, TRAI, CCI, electricity commissions) replaced direct control.
  • Business and politics: election funding debates (electoral bonds, struck down in 2024).
  • Federalism: states compete for investment; Finance Commission and GST Council become central forums.
The first wave in 1991 opened industry and trade. Later reforms built the rules of the market: regulators, bankruptcy law and a national tax.

• India's share of the world economy and status among the largest economies; debate on whether growth creates enough jobs.
  • GST 2.0 (September 2025) and compensation questions for states.
  • Labour codes (November 2025) and union protests.
  • 16th Finance Commission (2026-31).
  • Viksit Bharat 2047 goals through NITI Aayog.
  • Trade negotiations and tariffs in a protectionist world.

"Discuss the politics of economic reforms in India since 1991."
"Liberalisation has created a pro-business rather than pro-market state." Examine.
"Assess the impact of economic reforms on Indian federalism."

Structure: 1991 crisis; main measures; Jenkins, Varshney, Kohli; outcomes; later reforms (GST, IBC, labour codes); critiques; links to parties, welfare and federalism; balanced conclusion.
